name: Bulu (groupement Yekombo)
place: Yekɔmbo grouping, second-degree chiefdom of Mbom (South)
overview: In the majority in their grouping, in contact with the Ngoe and the Esse, the Bulu of Yekombo live from cocoa, food crops, fishing and basketry. Societies of families and hierarchical chiefdoms, they used to gather under the adum tree to consult the ancestors; Christianity has replaced these cults, but the cuisine, the eɲəŋə dance and the bikutsi remain.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, in contact with the Ngoe and the Esse, whose speech varieties it also speaks.
Bulu is spoken in Kribi, Ebolowa and as far as Gabon.
Rather mixed group; exogamy is the rule, in strict observance of kinship.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Land of the ancestors, which belongs to them; the group keeps no ties with other places of origin.
The land belongs to God; each family owns its inherited share, and there are community plots.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Families (head of family), villages (first-, second- and third-degree chiefs), notables: decisions are taken at each level, up to the sub-prefecture, by consensus after consulting the notables.
A widower and a widow may see each other freely; not an unmarried man and a married woman.
Permanent societies: mothers specialised in burying babies, and orators who speak at weddings and mourning.
The child is never right before his father; the wife owes respect to her husband.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband.
A boy becomes a man after twenty, when he has his house, his plantation, and gives the viper to his father.
Ages given: 25 for the man; for the woman, 17 today, younger in the past.
Steps: meeting, əkut mbe (introducing oneself), marriage proposal, bride price.
Bride price: envelope of money and wine (compensation), suit (keepsake), animal (billy goat, goat or pig), whose meaning is interpreted on the day itself.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Ancestral cults are no longer practised, replaced by Christianity.
The adum, a tree standing opposite the chiefdom, is the place where contact was made with the ancestors.
Birth is the return of a forebear; death, the return to the forebears.
Taboos: incest, the intimate life of the parents, palavers under the adum.
Taboos: a boy does not eat viper without his father's consent, nor certain birds (ŋgə'ə); a pregnant woman avoids snake meat and certain pieces; one does not speak insolently to elders.
Incest and witchcraft were punished by isolation.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: cocoa, basketry, sculpture, fishing. Women: food crops, fishing.
Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying harvests, mortars.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Formerly leopard skin, obom and a straw kaba ŋkuk; today, cloth.
Traditional medicine takes precedence over modern medicine.
Beauty: the robust, tall man with a flawless face; the natural woman, with dark skin, without make-up or skin lightening.
Courtship: offering bracelets, dancing well and playing the drum; the woman an excellent dancer and of good conduct.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: eɲəŋə, abok ɓəkon, bikutsi, bɔlo, maŋgambə; instruments: tam-tam, drum, balafon, guitar.
Dances: eɲəŋə at popular festivals, esani at times of mourning.
No community festival of its own.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Marriage, social organisation and taboos bring the Bulu close to the Fang; several ancestral practices have declined in the face of Christianity.

sections.title: The names
items: The father gives each child their name; in the event of separation, he may change it once.
People are addressed by their motto (eŋdán) and pet names; the appellative is marked by a high-low tone: Ǎndəmba for Ndəmba.
The founding ancestor, Ndəmba Owutu, means “here then is Mba”.

ethnonymes.meaning: Related to the Esa ntimba among the Faŋ of Djoum

lessons.title: Who are the Bulu (groupement Yekombo)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Majority group, in contact with the Ngoe and the Esse, whose speech varieties it also speaks. • Bulu is spoken in Kribi, Ebolowa and as far as Gabon. • A rather mixed group; exogamy is the rule, in strict respect of kinship. • Land of the ancestors, which belongs to them; the group keeps no ties with other places of origin. • The land belongs to God; each family owns its inherited share, and there are community plots.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in their grouping, in contact with the Ngoe and the Esse, the Bulu of Yekombo live from cocoa, food crops, fishing and basketry. Societies of families and hierarchical chiefdoms, they used to gather under the adum tree to consult the ancestors; Christianity has replaced these cults, but the cuisine, the eɲəŋə dance and the bikutsi remain.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Bulu (groupement Yekombo) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Bulu (groupement Yekombo) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Families (head of family), villages (chiefs of the 1st, 2nd and 3rd degree), notables: decisions are taken at each level, up to the sub-prefecture, by consensus after consulting the notables. • A widower and a widow may see each other freely; not so a bachelor and a married woman. • Permanent societies: mothers who specialise in burying babies, and speakers who take the floor at weddings and funerals. • The child is never right in front of his father; the wife owes respect to her husband.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Families (head of family), villages (first-, second- and third-degree chiefs), notables: decisions are taken at each level, up to the sub-prefecture, by consensus after consulting the notables. A widower and a widow may see each other freely; a single man and a married woman may not. Permanent societies: mothers who specialise in burying babies, and speakers who address the gathering at weddings and funerals.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: kpem (cassava leaves), miŋkonda (grated cassava and groundnut), saŋga (vegetables and maize), ebafon (maize and groundnut), bombo (maize cake). • Drinks: zɔŋ (aubergine infusion), palm wine. • Men: cocoa, basketry, sculpture, fishing. Women: food crops, fishing. • Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying harvests, mortars.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Bulu (groupement Yekombo) mainly eat kpem, miŋkonda, saŋga, ebafon. Traditional drinks: zɔŋ, palm wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo)
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Bulu (groupement Yekombo) family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Bulu (groupement Yekombo) family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The father gives each child their name; in case of separation, he may change it once. • People are addressed by their motto (eŋdán) and nicknames; the appellative is marked by a high-low tone: Ǎndəmba for Ndəmba. • The founding ancestor, Ndəmba Owutu, means “here then is Mba”. • Birth is the return of an ancestor; death, the return to the ancestors. • A boy becomes a man after twenty, when he has his house, his plantation, and offers the viper to his father.

steps.instruction: Among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo), traditional dances (eɲəŋə, esani) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam, drum, balafon.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Bulu (groupement Yekombo) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Bulu (groupement Yekombo). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Bulu (groupement Yekombo). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Men: cocoa, basketry, sculpture, fishing. Women: food crops, fishing. • Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying the harvests, mortars.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: cocoa, basketry, sculpture, fishing. Women: food crops, fishing. Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying harvests, mortars.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Ancestral cults are no longer practised, replaced by Christianity. • The adum, a tree standing opposite the chiefdom, is the place where contact was made with the ancestors. • Birth is the return of an ancestor; death, the return to the ancestors. • Taboos: incest, the parents' intimate life, palavers under the adum. • Prohibitions: a boy does not eat viper without his father's consent, nor certain birds (ŋgə'ə); a pregnant woman avoids snake meat and certain cuts; one does not speak insolently to elders.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Ancestral cults are no longer practised, having been replaced by Christianity. The adum, a tree standing in front of the chiefdom, is the place where people made contact with the ancestors.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

student.memo: Ancestral cults are no longer practised, having been replaced by Christianity. The adum, a tree standing in front of the chiefdom, is the place where people made contact with the ancestors.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Bulu
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Bulu (groupement Yekombo) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Bulu (groupement Yekombo) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Bulu. • Greeting formulae: mbolo = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); mbambatʃe = morning greeting (one person); Mbamba mos = midday greeting (one person). • Counting from 1 to 5: Fɔk, Baj, La, nin, tan. • The founding ancestor, Ndəmba Owutu, means “here, then, is Mba”. • Marriage, social organisation and taboos bring the Bulu close to the Fang; several ancestral practices have declined in the face of Christianity.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Bulu are the first steps towards communicating with the Bulu (groupement Yekombo). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Bulu.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Bulu are the first steps towards communicating with the Bulu (groupement Yekombo). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
